title: Placenta Praevia and Low-Lying Placenta: Surveillance and Delivery Planning

evidenceAudit.scope: Pregnant woman in whom the mid-pregnancy anomaly scan shows a placenta covering or within 20 mm of the internal cervical os: confirmation by transvaginal scan, follow-up scans at 32 and 36 weeks, home or hospital care in the third trimester, bleeding emergencies, antenatal corticosteroids, timing and place of caesarean birth, and when to suspect placenta accreta spectrum. Uses RCOG Green-top Guideline 27a for definitions, surveillance and delivery planning and a Saudi 10-year cohort for local risk patterns; no Saudi national guideline for placenta praevia was found.
findings: Every dose, threshold and timing was checked against the cited source section on 2026-10-20.
Normal values are typical adult reference ranges; laboratories differ.
unverifiedSections: No Saudi Ministry of Health or Saudi Society of Obstetrics and Gynecology guideline for placenta praevia was found; RCOG Green-top 27a (England) is the clinical source and the Saudi Medical Journal Abha cohort (2012-2021) supplies local risk patterns only.
The RCOG text used is the accepted final draft (Winter 2017) of the 2018 guideline; page locators are section numbers and the final published wording should be checked.

Betamethasone 12 mg intramuscularly as two doses 12 to 24 hours apart comes from an NHS trust guideline that follows RCOG practice; the Celestone Soluspan US label does not list antenatal use, so this use is off-label and the label supplies administration and contraindication detail only.
RCOG Green-top 27a advises one course of corticosteroids at 34+0 to 36+0 weeks; the exact gestation window used in Saudi hospitals was not verified.

Anti-D immunoglobulin dose for a bleeding episode is the Rhophylac sensitising-event dose (300 micrograms within 72 hours); a Kleihauer test and larger doses for large fetomaternal haemorrhage follow the label and local blood bank protocol.
Iron supplementation and transfusion thresholds are described as RCOG advice; no iron or blood product regimen is written because no label or Saudi protocol was read.

Tocolysis, tranexamic acid, uterotonics, balloon tamponade, cell salvage and the surgical technique for placenta accreta spectrum are described only as items for the specialist team; no regimen is written.
Normal and abnormal ultrasound thresholds follow RCOG: low-lying is 20 mm or less from the internal os after 16 weeks, and the cervical length cut-offs are research findings, not diagnostic criteria.
Differentials and patient education lines follow standard obstetric practice and were not drawn from a single source section.
Figures were read by automated extraction of web pages, PDF text and label text; spot-check each value against the source during clinical review.
SFDA: the Saudi Food and Drug Authority register returned an empty page from this environment, so registration of this product in Saudi Arabia was not verified; check the register before prescribing.

pathophysiology.summary: The placenta implants low in the uterus, so it lies over or near the internal cervical os; as the lower segment stretches in the third trimester the placental attachment shears and bleeds (RCOG Green-top 27a, Section 2 Background). A caesarean scar, assisted reproduction, smoking, older age and high parity increase the risk of the placenta lying low (RCOG Green-top 27a, Section 3; Saudi Medical Journal 2023, Results). Most low-lying placentas seen at the mid-pregnancy scan resolve by 32 weeks as the lower segment grows, so a repeat transvaginal scan is needed to decide who has persistent praevia (RCOG Green-top 27a, Section 4.2). Bleeding risk rises sharply near term: the risk of an emergency bleed is reported as 4.7% by 35 weeks, 15% by 36 weeks, 30% by 37 weeks and 59% by 38 weeks, which is why delivery is planned at 36 to 37 weeks in uncomplicated cases (RCOG Green-top 27a, Section 4.8). A placenta over a previous caesarean scar can invade the muscle (placenta accreta spectrum), which can cause torrential bleeding and hysterectomy at birth (RCOG Green-top 27a, Section 6; Saudi Medical Journal 2023, Results).

A placenta over a previous caesarean scar can invade the muscle (placenta accreta spectrum), which can cause torrential bleeding and hysterectomy at birth (RCOG Green-top 27a, Section 6; Saudi Medical Journal 2023, Results).

symptoms: Painless bright red vaginal bleeding, often first in the second or third trimester (RCOG Green-top 27a, Section 4.4).
Contractions or vague suprapubic period-like aches with spotting (RCOG Green-top 27a, Section 4.4).
Often no symptoms and found on the routine anomaly scan (RCOG Green-top 27a, Section 4.1).
physicalSigns: Soft, non-tender uterus; fetus often lying transverse or breech (clinical judgment).
Maternal pulse and blood pressure showing shock when bleeding is heavy (clinical judgment).
Do not do a digital vaginal examination when the placental site is not known (clinical judgment).
redFlags: Any vaginal bleeding, including spotting, in a woman with known praevia or low-lying placenta: attend hospital immediately (RCOG Green-top 27a, Section 4.4).
Contractions or period-like suprapubic pain: attend hospital immediately (RCOG Green-top 27a, Section 4.4).
Heavy bleeding with signs of shock: call for senior obstetric, anaesthetic and blood bank help and resuscitate (RCOG Green-top 27a, Section 5).

Previous caesarean section with an anterior placenta over the scar: assess for placenta accreta spectrum and plan birth in a unit with critical care and a transfusion service (RCOG Green-top 27a, Section 5 and Section 6).
Atypical red cell antibodies: discuss with the haematologist and blood bank before birth (RCOG Green-top 27a, Section 5).
precipitants: Previous caesarean section, and more caesareans increase the risk (RCOG Green-top 27a, Section 3).
Assisted reproductive technology and maternal smoking (RCOG Green-top 27a, Section 3).
Older age and high parity: the main risk factors in a Saudi cohort of 299 women with major praevia (Saudi Medical Journal 2023, Results).
Previous uterine surgery and multiple pregnancy (clinical judgment).

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Painful, hard uterus, often with a concealed bleed and fetal distress, and a placenta clear of the cervix on scan (clinical judgment).
Fetal vessels over the os with painless bleeding after rupture of membranes and fetal heart rate change; identified by colour Doppler on transvaginal scan (clinical judgment).
Bleeding from polyp, ectropion or infection seen on speculum examination once praevia is excluded by scan (clinical judgment).
Regular painful contractions with cervical change; praevia must be excluded before a vaginal examination (clinical judgment).
Loss of the clear zone, bladder wall interruption and lacunae on ultrasound in a woman with an anterior placenta and previous caesarean (RCOG Green-top 27a, Section 6).

clinicalManagement.title: Identify at the mid-pregnancy scan
actions: Check the placental site at the routine anomaly scan (RCOG Green-top 27a, Section 4.1).
If the placenta covers the os or lies within 20 mm, label it praevia or low-lying and arrange a follow-up scan at 32 weeks (RCOG Green-top 27a, Section 4.2).
Advise the woman to attend at once with any bleeding, and avoid vaginal examination and intercourse (RCOG Green-top 27a, Section 4.4).

clinicalManagement.title: Confirm with transvaginal scan
actions: Perform a transvaginal scan; it is safe and more accurate than abdominal scanning (RCOG Green-top 27a, Section 4.3).
If resolved, return to routine care; if persistent, continue the pathway (RCOG Green-top 27a, Section 4.2).
Check risk of placenta accreta spectrum when there is a previous caesarean section and an anterior placenta (RCOG Green-top 27a, Section 6).

clinicalManagement.title: Plan third-trimester care
actions: Asymptomatic women: counsel about preterm birth and haemorrhage, ensure someone to help and quick access to hospital (RCOG Green-top 27a, Section 4.4).
Women with recurrent bleeding: tailor admission to distance, transport, bleeding history, blood results and acceptance of blood products (RCOG Green-top 27a, Section 4.4).
Assess venous thromboembolism risk if admitted (RCOG Green-top 27a, Section 4.4).
Check haemoglobin, give iron if indicated, and record blood group and antibodies (RCOG Green-top 27a, Section 5).
Repeat transvaginal scan at about 36 weeks if still asymptomatic and persistent (RCOG Green-top 27a, Section 4.3).

clinicalManagement.title: Give corticosteroids and plan birth
clinicalManagement.timeframe: 34+0 to 36+0 weeks, or earlier if preterm birth is likely
actions: Offer one course of betamethasone (see medicines) (RCOG Green-top 27a, Section 4.6).
Plan caesarean birth at 36 to 37 weeks if uncomplicated, or 35+1 to 36+6 weeks if complicated (RCOG Green-top 27a, Section 4.8).
Discuss consent, indications for transfusion and hysterectomy, and any refusal of blood, and document the plan (RCOG Green-top 27a, Section 5).
Arrange birth in a unit with transfusion on site and access to critical care, with a senior obstetrician and anaesthetist (RCOG Green-top 27a, Section 5).

clinicalManagement.title: Manage a bleeding episode
actions: Assess airway, breathing, circulation; place two large intravenous lines; send blood for count, group and crossmatch (RCOG Green-top 27a, Section 5).
Monitor the mother and baby; give anti-D if rhesus D negative (see medicines).
Tocolysis may be used for 48 hours only to allow corticosteroids when the woman is stable; do not use it when delivery is indicated (RCOG Green-top 27a, Section 4.7).
Deliver by caesarean section if bleeding is heavy or fetal or maternal compromise develops (RCOG Green-top 27a, Section 4.8).

clinicalManagement.title: After birth
actions: Plan for postpartum haemorrhage with uterotonics, tranexamic acid and blood products as per the unit protocol (RCOG Green-top 27a, Section 5).
Give anti-D within 72 hours if the baby is rhesus D positive and the mother is rhesus D negative (Rhophylac label, Section 2).
Monitor blood loss, haemoglobin and signs of infection; offer venous thromboembolism prophylaxis per risk (RCOG Green-top 27a, Section 4.4).

regimens.indication: Fetal lung maturation before expected late preterm birth (off-label)
regimens.patientGroup: Pregnant women with placenta praevia or low-lying placenta at 34+0 to 36+0 weeks or at higher risk of earlier birth
regimens.dose: 12 mg per dose, two doses given 12 to 24 hours apart (Celestone Soluspan holds 3 mg betamethasone as sodium phosphate plus 3 mg as acetate per mL, 6 mg total per mL, so 12 mg is 2 mL). Dilution and preparation: shake well before use; do not dilute and do not mix with preservative-containing diluents (parabens, phenol), which can cause flocculation.
regimens.route: Deep intramuscular injection; never intravenous and never epidural (Celestone Soluspan label, Warnings)
regimens.duration: One course only; do not repeat routinely (RCOG Green-top 27a, Section 4.6)
adjustments: Off-label: the Celestone Soluspan US label lists no obstetric use; dose and interval are from an NHS trust guideline (Milton Keynes MIDW/GL/53, Section 3.1).
Diabetes: not a contraindication, but monitor glucose closely and add insulin per local protocol (Milton Keynes MIDW/GL/53).
Multiple-dose vial contains benzalkonium chloride; the label warns about benzyl alcohol preservative in premature infants (Celestone label, Dosage and Administration).
Infants should be observed for signs of hypoadrenalism after maternal corticosteroids (Celestone label, Pregnancy).
Live vaccines are contraindicated in patients on immunosuppressive doses (Celestone label, Precautions).
SFDA: the Saudi Food and Drug Authority register returned an empty page from this environment, so registration of this product in Saudi Arabia was not verified; check the register before prescribing.
monitoring: Maternal blood glucose, especially in diabetes (Milton Keynes MIDW/GL/53).
Neonatal hypoglycaemia after late preterm exposure (Milton Keynes MIDW/GL/53).
Signs of systemic infection or fungal infection (Celestone label, Warnings).
contraindications: Hypersensitivity to any component of the product (Celestone Soluspan label, Contraindications).
Idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura (intramuscular route) (Celestone Soluspan label, Contraindications).
Systemic fungal infection unless needed to control a drug reaction (Celestone Soluspan label, Warnings).

regimens.indication: Prevention of rhesus D sensitisation after antepartum bleeding
regimens.patientGroup: Rhesus D-negative pregnant women not already sensitised, with vaginal bleeding
regimens.dose: 300 micrograms (1,500 IU) as a single dose within 72 hours of the bleeding episode; larger or repeated doses if a large fetomaternal haemorrhage is found; a further 300 micrograms within 72 hours of birth if the baby is rhesus D positive or unknown. 1 microgram equals 5 IU: do not confuse the units. Dilution and preparation: none; use the prefilled syringe as supplied; bring to room temperature, inspect for particles, do not freeze, single use.
regimens.route: Intramuscular or intravenous injection; if intramuscular and more than 5 mL, divide the dose between sites; never subcutaneous; observe for at least 20 minutes (Rhophylac label, Section 2)
adjustments: Use the product label regimen; NICE and local protocols may differ in dose and schedule (Rhophylac label, Section 2).
Do not give live virus vaccines within 3 months (Rhophylac label, Section 7.1).
Passive anti-D may appear on later antibody screens (Rhophylac label, Section 5.2).
SFDA: the Saudi Food and Drug Authority register returned an empty page from this environment, so registration of this product in Saudi Arabia was not verified; check the register before prescribing.
monitoring: Observe for 20 minutes for hypersensitivity (Rhophylac label, Section 2).
Fetomaternal haemorrhage test to decide the dose (Rhophylac label, Section 2.2).
Cord blood group of the baby (Rhophylac label, Section 2.2).
contraindications: Anaphylactic or severe systemic reaction to human immune globulin (Rhophylac label, Section 4).
IgA deficiency with IgA antibodies and a past reaction to Rhophylac (Rhophylac label, Section 4).
Not for the newborn of a mother who received it postpartum (Rhophylac label, Section 4).

diagnosticCriteria.threshold: Placenta lies directly over the internal os (RCOG Green-top 27a, Section 4.2).
After 16 weeks, placental edge 20 mm or less from the internal os on transabdominal or transvaginal scan (RCOG Green-top 27a, Section 4.2).
Transvaginal scan at 32 weeks if praevia or low-lying at the anomaly scan; if still persistent and no symptoms, repeat at about 36 weeks (RCOG Green-top 27a, Section 4.2 and Section 4.3).
A single course at 34+0 to 36+0 weeks, and before 34+0 weeks if at higher risk of preterm birth (RCOG Green-top 27a, Section 4.6).
Uncomplicated praevia: 36 to 37 weeks; complicated praevia or low-lying placenta: late preterm, 35+1 to 36+6 weeks (RCOG Green-top 27a, Section 4.8).
Maternity unit with on-site blood transfusion and critical care access (RCOG Green-top 27a, Section 5).

guidelineComparison.title: Action by scan finding

rows.parameter: Placenta over the os at the anomaly scan (praevia)
values: Transvaginal scan at 32 weeks, again at about 36 weeks if persistent and asymptomatic (RCOG Green-top 27a, Section 4.2 and 4.3)

Caesarean birth at 36 to 37 weeks (RCOG Green-top 27a, Section 4.8)
Late preterm birth at 35+1 to 36+6 weeks in a unit with transfusion and critical care (RCOG Green-top 27a, Section 4.8 and 5)

guidelineComparison.note: Based on RCOG Green-top 27a; the Abha cohort found 68.5% of major degree cases delivered before 37 weeks.

teaching.scope: Pregnant woman in whom the mid-pregnancy anomaly scan shows a placenta covering or within 20 mm of the internal cervical os: confirmation by transvaginal scan, follow-up scans at 32 and 36 weeks, home or hospital care in the third trimester, bleeding emergencies, antenatal corticosteroids, timing and place of caesarean birth, and when to suspect placenta accreta spectrum. Uses RCOG Green-top Guideline 27a for definitions, surveillance and delivery planning and a Saudi 10-year cohort for local risk patterns; no Saudi national guideline for placenta praevia was found.
learningObjectives: Check the placental site at the anomaly scan and follow up with a transvaginal scan at 32 weeks.
Tell women with praevia to attend hospital at once with any bleeding or pain.
Offer one course of corticosteroids at 34+0 to 36+0 weeks.
Plan caesarean birth at 36 to 37 weeks in a unit with transfusion and critical care.
pitfalls: Doing a vaginal examination before the placental site is known.
Missing a repeat scan at 32 weeks.
Using tocolysis to prolong pregnancy when delivery is indicated.
Forgetting anti-D for a rhesus D-negative woman who bleeds.
Planning birth in a unit without transfusion or critical care.
keyPoints: Low-lying is 20 mm or less from the os after 16 weeks; praevia is over the os.
Most low-lying placentas move away by 32 weeks, so repeat the scan before labelling.
Uncomplicated praevia: caesarean at 36 to 37 weeks; complicated: 35+1 to 36+6 weeks.
Previous caesarean with an anterior placenta needs assessment for accreta.

patientEducation: Your placenta is low in the womb; many move up before 32 weeks.
Go to hospital at once for any bleeding, even spotting, contractions, or period-like aches.
Do not have sex and do not insert anything into the vagina.
Keep someone with you and a way to reach the hospital quickly.
Your baby is likely to be born by caesarean section around 36 to 37 weeks.
lifestyleAndDiet: Rest and avoid heavy lifting or strenuous activity if advised.
Take iron if advised and eat iron-rich foods.
Pack a hospital bag early and arrange childcare.
Plan transport to the hospital that can reach it quickly.
mdtReferrals: Obstetrician and gynaecologist; sonographer; midwife; anaesthetist; haematologist and blood bank; neonatologist; radiologist; critical care team; pharmacist; social worker.
dischargeCriteria: Placental site and follow-up scan dates recorded; corticosteroid course given or planned; blood group, antibodies and haemoglobin known; delivery date and place agreed; bleeding warning signs and hospital access explained; anti-D given if rhesus D negative.
nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Transvaginal scan at 32 weeks and, if persistent, about 36 weeks; antenatal visits at least every 2 weeks from 32 weeks; planned caesarean at 36 to 37 weeks (35+1 to 36+6 if complicated); check haemoglobin and blood loss after birth.
